title: Notice a breakdown, then reread to repair
statement: Teach comprehension monitoring as two steps, noticing a breakdown by trying to say what the part is about, then rereading to repair it, not as an abstract instruction to monitor.
detail: A reading course's review standard, citing IES videos on monitoring comprehension and on self-monitoring and self-correcting, makes monitoring a concrete routine: flag the breakdown with a confusion signal or the paraphrase test, then reread to repair it and retest (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D3-reading-architecture.md`, line 21). An instruction to monitor your understanding names a goal, not a behaviour, so a reader who is lost has no procedure to run (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/comprehension-monitoring-repair-routine.md`). Prediction items follow the same pattern: once the evidence arrives the learner updates the guess, rather than guessing once.

evidence.quote: Comprehension-monitoring is a concrete two-move routine — flag the breakdown (a confusion signal or the paraphrase test 'say it in your own words or you didn't get it') then reread-to-repair — not an abstract 'monitor your understanding'
Prediction items force an *update* after evidence ('I predicted a doctor… my prediction was wrong — what is he?'), not one-shot guessing
it names a goal, not a behavior, so a child who is failing to comprehend has no procedure to invoke
when a prediction was involved — explicitly update the wrong guess

citations.ref: Self-Monitor Understanding and Self-Correct Word-Reading Errors, REL Southeast video
